reference_drawer.title: 📖 Data Tables & Averages Reference Guide
reference_drawer.description: Key Data Organisation and Central-Tendency Rules:

items.rule: Frequency tells how many observations belong to a value or class interval.
For equal-width continuous classes, class width is the difference between consecutive lower class boundaries or consecutive upper class boundaries.
Inclusive intervals include both stated endpoints, while exclusive intervals are formed so adjacent classes meet without overlap.
items.example: \text{In an exclusive class }20\text{--}30,\ 20\text{ is included and }30\text{ is excluded}

items.rule: The class mark is the midpoint of a class interval and represents the class when estimating a grouped-data mean.
The arithmetic mean is the total of all observations divided by the number of observations.
For grouped data, multiply each class mark by its frequency, add the products, and divide by total frequency.
Choose a convenient assumed mean A, calculate deviations d_i=x_i-A, and use the weighted deviation formula.
Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies up to a class.
Sort the observations first. For odd n, take the middle observation; for even n, average the two middle observations.
The mode is the observation that occurs most frequently.
Mean, median, and mode each describe the centre of a data set but respond differently to repeated values and extreme observations.

concepts.title: 1. Frequency Tables & Class Intervals
concepts.subtitle: Organising Raw Data into Manageable Groups
concepts.summary: A frequency table records how many observations occur in each value or class interval. Grouping is especially useful when a data set is too large to inspect value by value.

points.text: Frequency: The number of observations in a value or interval.
Class Interval: A range used to group observations.
Class Width: The size of each equal-width interval.
Inclusive: Both stated endpoints are treated as class members under the given convention.
Exclusive: Adjacent intervals meet at a boundary without overlap.
Check: The total of all frequencies must equal the total number of observations.

concepts.trap: Do not count the class boundaries as observations. A class interval describes a range; its frequency counts actual data values inside that range.

concepts.title: 2. Class Marks
concepts.subtitle: The Midpoint Representative
concepts.summary: The class mark is the midpoint of a class interval. In grouped-data calculations, each class mark acts as a representative value for all observations in that class.

points.text: Midpoint: Add the lower and upper class limits and divide by 2.
Grouped Mean: Multiply each class mark by its frequency.
Equal Intervals: Class marks form an arithmetic sequence when class widths are equal.
Important: A class mark is a representative value, not necessarily an observation that actually appears in the original data.

concepts.trap: Do not use the class width as the class mark. Width measures the interval size; class mark identifies its midpoint.

concepts.title: 3. Cumulative Frequency
concepts.subtitle: Building Running Totals
concepts.summary: Cumulative frequency is obtained by adding frequencies successively. It tells how many observations lie at or below a class in a less-than table, or at or above a class in a more-than table.

points.text: Less-than CF: Add frequencies from the first class downward.
More-than CF: Start from the total frequency and subtract frequencies successively, or add from the end.
Median Class: Locate where the cumulative frequency first reaches or exceeds $\frac{N}{2}$ for grouped-data reasoning.
Final Check: The final less-than cumulative frequency must equal the total frequency.

concepts.trap: Do not reset the cumulative total at every class. Each cumulative frequency contains the frequencies accumulated from the beginning up to that class.

concepts.title: 4. Mean on Raw and Grouped Data
concepts.subtitle: Finding the Numerical Centre
concepts.summary: The arithmetic mean uses every observation. For grouped data, class marks approximate observations inside each class, so the grouped mean is a weighted average of class marks.

points.text: Raw Data: Add every observation and divide by the number of observations.
Direct Method: Use $\bar{x}=\frac{\sum f_ix_i}{\sum f_i}$ with class marks $x_i$.
Assumed Mean: Choose a convenient A to reduce repeated arithmetic.
Efficiency: Direct method is transparent; assumed mean is often faster when class marks are large but close together.

concepts.trap: Do not divide by the number of classes. The denominator of the grouped mean is total frequency, not the number of intervals.

concepts.title: 5. Mode & Median on Raw Data
concepts.subtitle: Finding the Most Typical and Middle Values
concepts.summary: The mode is the most frequent value. The median is found after sorting the data and selecting the middle position or averaging the two central values when the number of observations is even.

points.text: Mode: Look for the value with the greatest frequency.
Odd Number of Values: The median is the single middle observation.
Even Number of Values: The median is the average of the two middle observations.
Comparison: Mean uses every value, median depends on position, and mode depends on frequency.
Outliers: An unusually large or small value can pull the mean more strongly than the median.

concepts.trap: Never find the median from an unsorted data set. Position only has meaning after the values are arranged in order.
